concepts.text: Everyday advice to students (study hard, pick job-oriented subjects, 'suitable' subjects for girls or boys, follow family expectations) shows individual choices are shaped by social forces
Outcomes depend on effort but also on job markets, gender, family background and social class
Questions such as who decides what a 'good job' is show sociology asks about meanings people take for granted
Preview of the chapter: sociological imagination, plurality and inequality, what sociology is, its emergence in Europe and India, and its scope

sections.name: 1.2 The Sociological Imagination: the Personal Problem and the Public Issue

concepts.text: C. Wright Mills' idea of the sociological imagination: grasping the link between personal biography and wider history
Distinction between personal troubles of the milieu and public issues of social structure
Examples: unemployment, war or industrialisation turning private lives into products of large-scale change
Case of homelessness: a private hardship that is really a public issue linked to jobs and rural-urban migration
State responses to public issues, e.g. Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin as a housing scheme
Activity type: identify a personal problem and trace the public issue behind it
Each person belongs to many 'societies' at once (nation, language, religion, caste, tribe, region); which one is 'ours' depends on context
India's plurality: village and city, past and present traditions, many groups living side by side
Inequality between and within societies: unequal access to wealth, education, health, power and respect
Case of caste discrimination in everyday life (a Dalit man refused service at a village tea shop)
Amartya Sen's point that inequality has many dimensions beyond income
Activity type: use survey data (e.g. NFHS on sanitation) to find indicators of inequality
Definition: sociology is the systematic study of human social life, groups and societies, including our own behaviour as social beings
Sociology differs from philosophical and religious reflection: it studies how society actually works, not how it ought to be
Peter Berger's image of the sociologist as a spy who must report what is seen without bias
Sociology as a science bound by rules of evidence that others can check
Debates within sociology: natural-science versus interpretive models; quantitative versus qualitative methods
Sociologists' findings can be used in different ways; how knowledge is used is not itself a sociological question
Common sense offers naturalistic and individualistic explanations (e.g. poverty blamed on laziness)
Sociological explanation of poverty in terms of class structure, irregular work and low wages
Common sense is unreflective and does not question its own origins; sociology asks 'is this really so?'
Sociology reveals unsuspected connections, e.g. Kargil war compensation to widows leading to forced remarriage within the husband's family under patriliny
Activity type: explain an issue first in naturalistic terms, then sociologically

sections.name: 1.6 The Intellectual Ideas that went into the Making of Sociology

concepts.text: Influence of theories of natural evolution (Darwin): society compared to an organism whose parts perform functions
Early travellers' accounts and colonial administrators' reports as sources about 'other' societies
Classification of societies into stages (hunting-gathering, pastoral, agrarian, industrial) with the West assumed most advanced
Thinkers associated with this: Auguste Comte, Karl Marx, Herbert Spencer
The Enlightenment: reason, individualism and scientific method applied to human affairs
Poverty seen as a 'social problem' rather than natural fate; social surveys as an early method
Auguste Comte regarded as founder of sociology, believing it would aid human welfare

sections.name: 1.7 The Material Issues that went into the Making of Sociology

concepts.text: Industrial Revolution centred in England and the rise of industrial capitalism
Capitalism: private ownership, profit-seeking entrepreneurs, markets, and goods, services and labour as commodities
Pre-industrial life: village-based, hierarchical, close-knit (peasants, artisans, landlords)
Degradation of labour: workers cut off from guild, village and family
Growth of crowded industrial cities, slums, pollution and new impersonal social relations
Factory production and mechanical division of labour; Marx saw it as oppressive yet potentially liberating through collective organisation
Clock time replacing task-based rhythms of work ('time is money')
Comparison: Britain urbanised rapidly while colonial India saw people pushed back into agriculture
Activity types: compare work in a village, a factory and a call centre; study effects of industrial capitalism on Indian village and city life

sections.name: 1.8 Why Should We Study the Beginning and Growth of Sociology in Europe?

concepts.text: Issues like urbanisation and factory production are relevant to all modern societies, including India
India's history is entangled with British capitalism and colonialism
Global spread of Western capitalism: slavery of Africans and indentured Indian labour to plantations (Fiji, Surinam, West Indies, Mauritius)
Example: R.K. Laxman's account of the colonially shaped, mixed population of Mauritius

sections.name: 1.9 The Growth of Sociology in India

concepts.text: Colonialism was integral to modern capitalism; Western sociology must be read in light of colonial experience
Marx's observation that cheap English cloth ruined Indian handloom weavers
Colonial writers wrongly saw the Indian village as unchanging, a survival of early society
Western division between sociology (modern societies) and social anthropology (simple societies) is blurred in India
M.N. Srinivas: in a diverse society like India 'the other' lives next door
Indian social anthropology moved from 'primitive' peoples to peasants, castes, ethnic groups, classes and industrial society

sections.name: 1.10 The Scope of Sociology and its Relationship to other Social Science Disciplines

concepts.text: Scope ranges from micro interactions (shopkeeper-customer, teacher-student) to macro and global processes
Sociology is defined more by how it studies than by what it studies
Boundaries between social sciences are overlapping; feminist theory argues for interdisciplinarity
Sociology and economics: economics studies production and distribution; sociology places economic behaviour in its social setting of norms and values
Political economy approach and feminist economics (counting unpaid domestic work); Bourdieu's call to count all social costs
Advertising and consumption as culturally shaped economic behaviour

Sociology and political science: political science focused on theory and government; political sociology studies voting, parties, decision-making, gender in politics; Max Weber as political sociologist
Sociology and history: history studies past events in concrete detail; sociology studies the recent past, abstracts and generalises; rise of social history
Sociology and psychology: psychology studies individual behaviour; social psychology bridges the two; Durkheim's study of suicide rates as social facts
Sociology and social anthropology: anthropology's branches; long fieldwork and ethnography versus surveys and questionnaires
Critique of Western anthropology's unequal relation with the 'natives'; colonialism blurred the idea of bounded simple societies
Indian sociology borrows from both traditions because India mixes tradition and modernity, village and city, caste and tribe, class and community
Activity types: how each discipline would study fashion, markets or elections; Santhal tea workers in Assam
Capitalism: market enterprise based on private ownership of the means of production
Dialectic: interplay of opposing social forces, e.g. constraint and individual will
Empirical investigation, social constraint and values as key terms
Explain why studying the origin and growth of sociology matters
Discuss different aspects of 'society' and contrast sociological with common-sense understanding
Discuss how social science disciplines borrow from one another
Apply the sociological imagination to a personal problem of yours or someone you know

chapters.title: Introducing Sociology: Terms, Concepts and their Use in Sociology

sections.name: 2.1 Introduction: Why Do We Need Special Terms and Concepts?

concepts.text: Sociology needs precise concepts because everyday words like 'group' or 'society' are vague
Concepts organise observations, allow comparison across societies and form building blocks of theory
Concepts carry the stamp of the debates and social contexts in which they arose
Two broad perspectives on society: functionalist (order, interdependence) and conflict (inequality, power)
Micro versus macro levels and the individual-society relationship (conceptual dualities)
Social group: people who interact regularly, share norms and goals, and have a sense of belonging
Aggregates or quasi-groups (crowd at a bus stop, people in a stadium) lack structure; they can turn into groups
Primary groups: small, face-to-face, intimate and lasting (family, close friends); C.H. Cooley
Secondary groups: larger, impersonal, goal-oriented, formal (offices, unions, political parties)
Community versus society/association: personal, emotional ties versus impersonal, contractual ties (Tönnies' Gemeinschaft and Gesellschaft)
In-groups and out-groups: 'we' versus 'they' feeling (W.G. Sumner); boundaries can change
Reference groups: groups whose standards we use to judge ourselves and aspire to copy (e.g. colonial-era Indian middle class copying British manners)
Peer groups: primary groups of people of similar age or status; peer pressure
Activity type: classify groups you belong to as primary/secondary, in-group/out-group, reference group
Definition: structured, persistent inequality between groups ranked by access to material or symbolic rewards
Stratification is a social, not individual or natural, feature and is passed across generations
Systems of stratification: slavery, caste, estates and class (open versus closed systems)
Caste: ascribed at birth, hereditary occupation, endogamy, purity-pollution ranking, little mobility
Class: economic, open, based on wealth, income and occupation; mobility possible
Life chances and social mobility differ by position in the stratification system
Gender and ethnicity as cross-cutting dimensions of inequality
Status: a socially defined position with rights and duties (e.g. mother, teacher, student)
Ascribed status (given by birth: age, caste, sex) versus achieved status (earned: doctor, athlete)
Status as prestige: social ranking of positions and occupations
Role: the expected behaviour attached to a status; status is occupied, role is played
Role set (Merton): the cluster of roles linked to a single status
Role conflict: clashing expectations from two or more statuses (e.g. working mother)
Role stereotyping: fixing roles to groups, e.g. men as breadwinners and women as homemakers
Social roles and statuses are not fixed; they are contested and change with society
Social control: ways society regulates behaviour of individuals and groups to maintain order
Functionalist view (control for order and stability) versus conflict view (control as a tool of dominant groups)
Formal social control: codified, by agencies like law, police, courts, state
Informal social control: personal and unofficial, through family, religion, kinship, custom, gossip, ridicule
Sanctions: positive (rewards) and negative (punishments) to enforce norms
Deviance: behaviour that departs from accepted norms; what counts as deviant varies across societies
Examples of control in schools, workplaces and communities
Why do sociologists need special terms and concepts?
Identify groups you belong to and classify them; compare primary and secondary groups
Describe how stratification operates in your society and how it affects you
Explain social control and give examples of formal and informal control in different spheres
Identify your roles and statuses; explain role conflict and role stereotyping with examples
Social institutions: lasting patterns of norms, beliefs, values and roles that meet social needs
Institutions both constrain individuals and open opportunities for them
Formal institutions (law, state, education) versus informal ones (family, religion, custom)
Functionalist view: institutions meet society's needs; conflict view: institutions favour dominant groups
Micro (family) and macro (state, economy) institutions are interlinked
Family as a group of people linked by kin ties with adult members responsible for children
Nuclear family (couple and children) versus extended/joint family (several generations or couples)
Functionalist view of nuclear family as suited to industrial society; critique of this view
Family is linked with economy, polity and culture; changes in one affect the others (e.g. falling marriage rates in former East Germany after unification)
Diverse family forms by residence: matrilocal versus patrilocal
By descent/inheritance: matrilineal versus patrilineal
By authority: matriarchal versus patriarchal
Gender inequality within the family: son preference, declining child sex ratio
Marriage as a socially sanctioned union; forms: monogamy (including serial monogamy) and polygamy
Polygamy types: polygyny (one husband, many wives) and polyandry (one wife, many husbands) and conditions linked to them
Rules of mate selection: endogamy (within a group like caste) and exogamy (outside a group like clan or village)
Arranged marriage, love marriage and changing practices; widowhood
Kinship: ties by blood (consanguineal) and by marriage (affinal)
Family of orientation (born into) versus family of procreation (formed through marriage)
Activity types: map your kinship terms; compare family forms across regions
Work: carrying out tasks with mental and physical effort to produce goods and services; paid and unpaid
Informal economy and unpaid domestic work as often-unrecognised forms of work
Modern forms of work and the division of labour: specialisation and interdependence
Industrial production in factories and the separation of home and workplace
Transformation of work: mass production, assembly lines (Fordism) and scientific management
Flexible production, outsourcing and globalisation (e.g. garment workers supplying global retailers)
Insecurity of work: low wages, contract labour, decline of permanent jobs
Political institutions concern the acquisition and distribution of power
Power: ability to carry out one's will even against resistance; seen as a fixed quantity
Authority: legitimate power accepted as just
Stateless societies: order maintained through kinship, age-sets and rituals without a formal state
The state: political apparatus ruling a territory with laws backed by force
Functionalist view of the state (serving all) versus conflict view (serving dominant classes)
Sovereignty: undisputed political rule over a territory
Citizenship: civil, political and social rights and corresponding duties
Nationalism: sense of belonging to a political community; struggles for rights expand democracy
Activity type: find examples of social movements that expanded citizens' rights
Sociological study of religion is empirical, comparative and non-judgemental, unlike theology
Features of religion: shared beliefs and rituals, sacred symbols, a community of believers
Durkheim's distinction between the sacred and the profane
Religion is linked with other institutions: power, politics and social stratification
Max Weber: Calvinist ethic of hard work and frugality contributed to the rise of capitalism
Religion and gender; religion and social change, e.g. anti-caste and reform movements
Secularisation thesis and the continuing public importance of religion
Education as a lifelong process; schooling as its formal, institutionalised form
Durkheim on education transmitting society's shared norms and values
Simple societies educate through community life; complex societies need formal schooling
Universalistic values in schools versus particularistic values of family and kin
Functionalist view: education prepares and allocates people to occupations
Conflict view: education reproduces social inequality (elite versus deprived schools, hidden curriculum)
Unequal access by class, caste and gender, e.g. dropout of SC/ST girls
Note how you are constrained and enabled by social institutions
Compare the main features of nuclear and joint families; explain types of marriage and residence rules
Explain the relationship between family and other social spheres
Explain power, authority and the state; compare stateless and state societies
Discuss religion and education as social institutions with examples
Culture as a 'map' or toolkit that guides how people behave and interpret the world
Culture is learned, shared and changing; cultures cannot be ranked but judged as adequate for their settings
Socialisation as the process through which we learn culture and become social beings
Different environments produce different cultures, e.g. island communities surviving the 2004 tsunami through traditional knowledge
Everyday versus sociological meaning of culture: not just 'high culture' but the whole way of life
Non-verbal culture and shared codes of communication (gestures, signals)
Edward Tylor: culture as the complex whole of knowledge, belief, art, morals, law, custom and capabilities
Bronislaw Malinowski: culture includes artefacts, goods, technical processes, ideas and habits; pioneer of fieldwork (Trobriand Islands)
Clifford Geertz: culture as webs of meaning through which people interpret experience
Other definitions (Kroeber and Kluckhohn, Leslie White) emphasising shared learned behaviour and symbols
Three dimensions: cognitive, normative and material
Cognitive dimension: how we make sense of information; oral versus literate cultures; changing role of literacy
Normative dimension: rules of conduct - folkways, mores, customs, conventions and laws
Norms are implicit, laws are explicit and formally enforced; norms vary by status and can discriminate
Sanctions as means of enforcing norms
Material dimension: tools, technology, artefacts and their use
Culture lag (W.F. Ogburn): non-material culture changing slower than material culture
Identity is socially formed through the roles we play and groups we belong to
Each role has shared codes understood by role-players
Sub-cultures: distinct styles, tastes and values of groups within a larger culture (e.g. youth groups)
Ethnocentrism: judging other cultures by the standards of one's own, assumed superior
Arises when cultures come into contact; example of colonial attitudes (Macaulay's Minute, 1835)
Cosmopolitanism: valuing other cultures and openly borrowing from them
Examples of cultural borrowing: English absorbing foreign words, Hindi film music, Hinglish
Cultural change through internal causes (new ideas, inventions) and external causes (contact, conquest)
Natural or ecological change as a source of cultural change
Evolutionary (slow) versus revolutionary (sudden) cultural change, e.g. the French Revolution
Definition: lifelong process by which a helpless infant becomes a self-aware, knowledgeable person
Cases of isolated or 'feral' children showing the need for socialisation
Primary socialisation (early childhood, family) versus secondary socialisation (school, work, wider society)
Re-socialisation: unlearning and relearning norms in new settings
Socialisation is not mere programming; individuals actively interpret and respond
Family: varying family systems, region and class shape what children learn
Peer groups: relations among equals, age-grades, peer pressure
School: formal curriculum and hidden curriculum (e.g. gender roles)
Mass media: print, television and digital media; debates on their effects
Other agencies: workplace, neighbourhood, caste/class, region and religion
Gendered socialisation: boys and girls raised to different expectations (Krishna Kumar's 'Growing up Male'; story 'The Bell')
Agencies of socialisation can conflict with one another
Socialisation is also the source of individuality and independent thinking
Explain how the sociological understanding of culture differs from everyday usage
Show how the dimensions of culture are interrelated
Compare ethnocentrism and cosmopolitanism; explain why cosmopolitanism suits modern societies
Compare evolutionary and revolutionary approaches to cultural change
Identify the socialising agents in your life and describe their role

chapters.title: Understanding Society: Social Change and Social Order in Rural and Urban Society

concepts.text: Rapid, continuous social change is recent: it covers only the last few centuries of human history (Giddens' clock analogy)
Social change must be studied together with social order, which resists and regulates it
Activity type: list things that did not exist in your grandparents' youth and things that have vanished
Social change means significant change: intensive (deep) and extensive (affecting many people)
Classifying change by nature or speed: evolutionary change (slow, Darwin's idea; social Darwinism) versus revolutionary change (rapid, often political)
Classifying by impact: structural change (e.g. shift to paper money) versus change in ideas and values (e.g. ideas of childhood and child labour)
Environmental causes: geography, climate and natural disasters (desert, cold and river-valley societies; 2004 tsunami); discovery of oil in West Asia
Technological and economic causes: steam power, railways, textile mills, plantations and world trade rules (WTO)
Political causes: wars, conquests, independence movements, end of monarchies, universal adult franchise
Cultural causes: religion and ideas, e.g. Weber's Protestant ethic, Bhakti, changing status of women, sport such as cricket
Social order: patterns of behaviour that persist and resist change
Dominant groups tend to favour stability while subordinate groups seek change
Order maintained by spontaneous consent through shared values and socialisation, and by coercion
Activity type: imagine life if rules changed every day
Power: ability to make others do what one wants; domination: stable exercise of power
Legitimacy: acceptance of power as just; authority (Weber) as legitimate power
Law: explicit codified norms enforced by the state; examples of authority (judge, police officer, teacher)
Informal authority of religious or sect leaders
Contestation: dissent and disagreement with established order; counter-cultures and elections
Crime as an act that breaks a law; laws can be unjust and deliberately broken (Gandhi's salt satyagraha)
Violence as the extreme form of contestation; the state claims a monopoly over legitimate violence (Weber)
Villages emerged with settled agriculture and the production of surplus
Rural-urban distinction based on population density and share of agricultural occupations
Census definitions: town, urban agglomeration and metropolitan area
Trends in India's urbanisation and growth of large cities

sections.name: 5.8 Social Order and Social Change in Rural Areas

concepts.text: Villages have stronger social order: small size, face-to-face ties, little anonymity and dependence on dominant groups
Traditional power structures: dominant landowning castes (Srinivas) control land, labour and local institutions
Land reforms and their effects on rural power
Technological change in agriculture (irrigation, machines, new seeds) altering labour relations
State development programmes and employment schemes in rural areas (e.g. rural employment guarantee)
Activity type: study a rural employment scheme's aims and problems

sections.name: 5.9 Social Order and Social Change in Urban Areas

concepts.text: Urbanism as a way of life: anonymity, individualism and diversity
Centrality of space in cities: who lives where, and segregation by class, caste, religion or ethnicity
Slums and the problems of housing and services for the urban poor
Ghettoisation: concentration of a community in an area, often for security
Gated communities: enclosed affluent enclaves with private services
Transport and commuting: long commutes, local trains and metro systems
Gentrification: upgrading of poor neighbourhoods displacing earlier residents
Activity types: study gated communities and ask who gains and loses from gentrification
Explain why social change is hard to define and give its types
Explain the role of environment, technology/economy, politics and culture in social change
Explain the link between social change and social order; how order is maintained
Distinguish domination, authority and law; explain contestation and crime
Compare social order and change in rural and urban areas; discuss urban space issues
Sociology was born in 19th-century Western Europe as a product of the 'age of revolutions'
The Enlightenment: rise of reason, secular, scientific and humanistic thinking; individual as knower
The French Revolution (1789): political sovereignty, liberty, equality and fraternity; end of feudal bonds; separation of public and private
The Industrial Revolution: science and technology applied to production; new organisation of labour and markets
Social effects of industrialisation: factories, urban poverty, slums, new state responsibilities for health and sanitation
Sociology as the 'science of the new industrial society' responding to the need for knowledge about it
Marx's life and works, including the Communist Manifesto (with Engels) and Capital
Aim of ending exploitation through 'scientific socialism'; critique of capitalism
Economic structure (base) as the foundation of society, shaping the superstructure of ideas, law and politics
Means of production, relations of production and mode of production
Stages of history: primitive communism, slavery, feudalism, capitalism, and the expected transition to socialism
Classes defined by position in the production process; shared interests of class members
Capitalism's two main classes: bourgeoisie (owners of means of production) and working class (sell labour for wages)
Class consciousness developing through political mobilisation
Class struggle as the driving force of history; revolution as overthrow of the ruling class
Alienation of workers under capitalist production
Durkheim's life and works: The Division of Labour in Society, Rules of Sociological Method, Suicide, Elementary Forms of Religious Life
Founder of sociology as a formal academic discipline with its own subject matter
Social facts: ways of acting and thinking external to the individual and exercising constraint; to be studied scientifically
Society as a moral system; social solidarity and its observable indicators such as law
Division of labour explains the shift from simple to modern societies
Mechanical solidarity: based on likeness and a strong collective conscience in small, simple societies; repressive law
Organic solidarity: based on difference and interdependence in large modern societies; restitutive law
Growth of population density increasing the division of labour and weakening collective conscience
Greater individual autonomy and voluntary associations in modern society
Weber's life and works, including The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism
Interpretive sociology: understanding the subjective meaning of social action
Social sciences need methods different from natural sciences
Empathetic understanding (Verstehen): putting oneself in the actor's place
Value neutrality: describing others' values without judging them
Ideal type: a logically consistent model highlighting key features, used as an analytical tool, not a description
Three types of authority: traditional, charismatic and rational-legal
Bureaucracy as the typical organisation of rational-legal authority; separation of public office and private life
Features of bureaucracy: fixed jurisdiction of officials, hierarchy of positions, reliance on written files, trained specialised office management, disciplined full-time conduct in office
Why did the Enlightenment, French Revolution and Industrial Revolution shape sociology?
Explain Marx's idea of class struggle and the role of economic structure
Compare mechanical and organic solidarity; how does law indicate the type of solidarity?
Explain Weber's interpretive sociology, ideal type and value neutrality
Describe the features of bureaucracy and compare with other organisations you know
Sociology in India began under colonial rule: teaching from 1919 at Bombay, then Calcutta and Lucknow
Early questions: colonial modernity, the relevance of anthropology to India, and sociology's role in nation-building
Indianising the discipline: each founder took a distinct approach
Studying founders critically so that later generations can build on them

sections.name: 7.2 The Pioneers: L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer and Sarat Chandra Roy

concepts.text: Many early Indian anthropologists entered the field by accident
L.K. Ananthakrishna Iyer: clerk-teacher turned ethnographer of Cochin; helped set up the first post-graduate anthropology department at Calcutta
Sarat Chandra Roy: Ranchi lawyer and court interpreter; studied the Oraon, Munda and Kharia; founded the journal 'Man in India'
Administrator-anthropologists of colonial India (Risley, Thurston, Hutton, Crooke) and their surveys and censuses
Ghurye as founder of institutionalised sociology: headed Bombay department, founded Indian Sociological Society and Sociological Bulletin
Biography: studied under Rivers and Haddon at Cambridge; Ph.D. published as Caste and Race in India
Influences: diffusionism, Orientalist scholarship on Hinduism, nationalism
Tribe debate: British protectionists wanted to isolate tribes; nationalists wanted them integrated into the mainstream
Ghurye's view of tribes as 'backward Hindus' who had long interacted with Hindu society
Risley's racial theory of caste using anthropometry: upper castes Aryan, lower castes non-Aryan
Ghurye's critique: the theory fits only north India; racial mixture elsewhere; averages hide variation

Ghurye's six features of caste: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on social interaction (food, purity-pollution), differential rights and duties, restricted choice of occupation, restrictions on marriage (endogamy)
Activity type: link the tribal debate to tribal movements, new states and displacement by dams and mines
Mukerji as part of the Lucknow school with Radhakamal Mukerjee and D.N. Majumdar; biography and key works
Argument that India had too much 'society'; sociologists must be rooted in Indian social traditions
Living tradition: a tradition that keeps links with the past while adapting to the new
Change in India comes through group and caste experience rather than class conflict
Three principles of change in Indian tradition: shruti, smriti and anubhava (experience), the last being revolutionary
Collective experience of Bhakti and Sufi saints as an example of anubhava
Activity type: trace changes in games, festivals or dress across generations
Desai as a Marxist sociologist; key works such as Social Background of Indian Nationalism
Welfare state: a positive (interventionist) state, democratic, with a mixed economy
Desai's tests of a welfare state: freedom from poverty, discrimination and insecurity; reduced income inequality; community needs over profit; stable development; full employment
Desai's verdict: the welfare state is largely a myth even in advanced capitalist countries; he also criticised communist states
Activity type: list state services in your area and how different classes view them
Srinivas' training under Ghurye and at Oxford (Radcliffe-Brown, Evans-Pritchard); institutions he built (Baroda, Delhi School of Economics, Bangalore)
Village studies as a central field of Indian sociology in the 1950s-60s (Srinivas, S.C. Dube, D.N. Majumdar)
Concepts linked to Srinivas: dominant caste and Sanskritisation
Debate with Louis Dumont: Dumont saw the village as a mere collection of people and caste as the real unit
Srinivas' view: the village was a real social unit, had changed historically and was never a self-sufficient 'little republic'
Significance of village studies: showed value of ethnographic fieldwork and documented rapid rural change in a new nation
Activity types: identify clues that a place is a village; discuss whether urban Indians still care about villages
Anthropometry, assimilation, endogamy, exogamy, laissez-faire, living tradition and welfare state as key terms
How did Iyer and Roy come to practise social anthropology?
State the arguments on both sides of the tribal debate
Compare Risley's and Ghurye's positions on caste and race; outline the features of caste
Explain D.P. Mukerji's 'living tradition'
Explain the welfare state and Desai's criticism of it
Compare Srinivas and Dumont on the village; explain the significance of village studies
